event_info.event_description: Analyze for disclosures on global pandemic risks. Look for corporate language discussing widespread impacts like supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, remote work transitions, and fundamental shifts in consumer demand.

holistic_analysis: LDOS’s 2021-02-23 Form 10-K frames COVID-19 as one of the most acute and multifaceted risks confronting the company.  The disclosure is recent (within one year of the pandemic’s declaration), so the Time Decay Principle allows high severity scores.  Management moves beyond boiler-plate language by documenting both already-experienced impacts (e.g., sharp fall-off in airport security product demand, contract execution delays, higher programme costs) and a broad set of forward-looking exposures (work-force outages, uncertain vaccine roll-out, possible recessionary after-effects, supply-chain fragility, and budget re-prioritisation by its government-agency customers).  Although LDOS references some mitigation (remote-work protocols, potential CARES Act recovery), these actions are described as uncertain or partial, and no quantified offsets are provided.  The narrative therefore depicts a live, continuing threat that has already eroded revenues and profitability and could further weaken operations, cash-flow and government funding flows.  Given this immediacy, specificity and breadth of impact, the extracted evidence generally earns upper-mid to high scores (4-7), capped below 10 because most statements remain qualitative and lack precise financial magnitudes.

evidence_list.snippet: The extent to which our business will be adversely affected by COVID-19 or other health epidemics, pandemics and similar outbreaks is highly uncertain and cannot be predicted.

components.reason: Explicitly names COVID-19 as a potential adverse impact on the business.
Highlights high uncertainty and unpredictability, signalling uncontrollable downside risk.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Directly acknowledges pandemic risk and uncertainty but remains generic, so mid-level score.

evidence_list.snippet: The outbreak and global spread of COVID-19, and the preventative or protective actions that governments, corporations, individuals and we are taking and may continue to take in an effort to limit the impact of COVID-19, have resulted in a period of business disruption and increased economic uncertainty.

components.reason: States that COVID-19 has already produced ‘business disruption’.
Connects pandemic to ‘increased economic uncertainty’, broadening the risk horizon.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Describes realised disruption and macro-economic uncertainty, but still qualitative; high-mid score.

evidence_list.snippet: The spread of COVID-19 has caused us to modify our business practices (including employee travel, access to customer sites, employee and contractor remote work and cancellation of physical participation in meetings, events and conferences), and we may take further actions as may be required by government authorities or that we determine are in the best interests of our employees, customers and business partners.

components.reason: Details concrete operational adjustments already made (remote work, travel curbs).
Signals possibility of additional, unspecified actions implying ongoing disruption.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Shows present operational impact; mentions future actions but no hard financials—moderate-high risk.

evidence_list.snippet: If significant portions of our workforce are unable to work effectively, including because of illness, quarantines, government actions, facility closures or other restrictions due to COVID-19, our operations and results will likely be impacted.

components.reason: Connects workforce health restrictions directly to impacts on operations and results.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Clear causal link between COVID-19 labour disruption and financial results; qualitative but strong.

evidence_list.snippet: In particular, a delay in wide distribution of vaccines, or a lack of public acceptance of vaccines, could lead people to continue to self-isolate and not participate in the economy at pre-pandemic levels for a prolonged period of time.

components.reason: Highlights dependency on vaccine rollout; delay prolongs economic drag on demand.
Specifies behavioural change (continued self-isolation) extending risk horizon.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Forward-looking risk tied to vaccination pace; important but less immediate or company-specific.

evidence_list.snippet: Even after COVID-19 has subsided, we may experience materially adverse impacts on our business as a result of the pandemic's global economic impact, including any recession that is occurring or may occur in the future.

components.reason: Projects ‘materially adverse’ impacts persisting post-pandemic.
Links risk to broader potential recession, amplifying severity.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Extends risk into future recessionary scenario; strong wording but still unquantified.

evidence_list.snippet: For example, the global spread of COVID-19 has resulted in a substantial decline in demand for air travel, which has adversely impacted the demand for products and services related to our airport security detection and automation business.

components.reason: Provides concrete example of pandemic causing ‘substantial decline’ in a specific revenue stream.
Identifies affected business line (airport security detection and automation).
Acknowledges actual adverse impact already being felt.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Most specific evidence—names line of business and describes realised, severe demand drop; high score.

evidence_list.snippet: Further, new contract awards have been and may continue to be delayed and our ability to perform on our existing contracts has been and may continue to be delayed or impaired, which will negatively impact our revenues.

components.reason: States that both new and existing contracts are already delayed.
Links delays directly to negative revenue impact.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Connects pandemic to revenue erosion through contract delays; credible, company-specific risk.

evidence_list.snippet: In addition, our program costs have increased and may continue to increase as a result of COVID-19, and these cost increases may not be fully recoverable or adequately covered by insurance, or equitable adjustments to contract prices or reimbursement of costs under Section 3610 of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security Act, which could impact our profitability.

components.reason: Notes realised cost inflation attributable to COVID-19.
Warns that recovery mechanisms may be inadequate, threatening profitability.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Highlights actual cost overruns and limited recovery prospects—direct profitability risk; high-mid score.

evidence_list.snippet: The continued spread of COVID-19 has had and may continue to have similar negative impacts on our customers, subcontractors, service providers and suppliers, causing delay or limiting their ability to perform, including in making timely payments to us.

components.reason: Describes knock-on effects across supply chain and payment cycles.
States impacts are both current (‘has had’) and prospective (‘may continue’).

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Addresses systemic supply-chain and liquidity risks; meaningful though not quantified.

evidence_list.snippet: Any resulting financial impact cannot be reasonably estimated at this time but may materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows.

components.reason: Warns of material adverse effect across multiple financial metrics.
Emphasises uncertainty of magnitude, signalling wide downside range.

evidence_list.reasoning_summary: Captures breadth of potential damage but remains abstract and unquantified, yielding a moderate score.
